title: So and not as substitutes for clauses, etc.
subtitle: I'd imagine so / I guess not
summary: Use so and not in place of a whole clause after verbs of thinking and speaking, and in short answers.

lesson.heading: so instead of an adjective, an adverb or a clause
lesson.text: So can stand for an adjective, an adverb or a whole clause that has just been mentioned, so that we don't have to repeat it.

examples.text: The workers were angry and they had every right to be **so**.
Joe took the work seriously and Petra perhaps even more **so**.
Usman's giving us a lift. At least I presume **so**.
examples.note: so = that he's giving us a lift

lesson.heading: Verbs of thinking and speaking
lesson.text: We often use so instead of a clause after verbs concerned with thinking and speaking. After tell we need an indirect object.

examples.text: *A:* Is Lewis going back to Scotland to see his parents this summer? *B:* I've no idea, but I'd imagine **so**. He goes most years.
I found it ridiculous, and said **so**. / ... and told them **so**.
examples.note: so = that I found it ridiculous

lesson.note: Also: be afraid (expressing regret), appear / seem (after 'it'), assume, believe, expect, guess, hope, presume, suppose, suspect, think.

lesson.heading: Verbs that don't take so
lesson.text: Some other verbs of thinking and speaking are never followed by so. With them we use it, or we spell the clause out.

examples.text: *A:* Will Stefan know how to mend it? *B:* I doubt **it**. / I doubt (that) he will.

lesson.note: Also: accept, admit, agree, be certain, hear, know, promise, suggest, be sure. In informal English, particularly in an argument, 'I know so' is possible.

lesson.heading: Negatives: not or not ... so
lesson.text: In negative sentences we use either not on its own or a negative verb + so. Which one depends on the verb.

examples.text: Is the Socialist Party offering anything new in its statement? It would appear **not**.
They want to buy the house, although they **didn't say so** directly.

lesson.heading: Which verbs take which negative
rows: *A:* I don't suppose there'll be any seats left. *B:* No, I **don't suppose so**. (or ... I **suppose not**.)
*A:* Will we need to show our passports? *B:* I **don't think so**.
be afraid, assume, guess, hope, presume, suspect
*A:* You'd better do it yourself. Eva won't help. *B:* No, I **guess not**.
lesson.note: With believe, expect, imagine and think, 'I think not' is possible but rather formal. With guess we don't say ~~I don't guess so~~.

lesson.heading: said not, said not to and didn't say so

left.label: *The teacher said not (to).*
left.text: The teacher gave us that information.
examples: *A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher **said not**. (= the teacher said that we didn't have to)
*A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher **said not to**. (= the teacher said that we shouldn't)

right.label: *The teacher didn't say so.*
right.text: The teacher gave us no such information - so perhaps we should.
examples: *A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher **didn't say so**.

lesson.heading: Short answers: So it has. or Yes, it has.

left.label: So + pronoun + auxiliary - news to me
left.text: We use this when we can see that something is true now that we have been told, particularly if we are surprised.
examples: *A:* Lisa and Sara are here. *B:* **So they are**. (or Yes, they are.)
*A:* Your bike's been moved. *B:* **So it has**. I wonder who did it.

right.label: Yes, ... - I knew already
right.text: If we knew before being told, only Yes, ... is possible.
examples: *A:* Your bike's been moved. *B:* **Yes, it has**. Philip borrowed it this morning.
not ~~So it has. Philip borrowed it this morning.~~

lesson.heading: So I gather / So I hear
lesson.text: With verbs like appear (after 'it'), believe, gather, hear, say, seem, tell and understand, a short answer with so + subject + verb implies 'I knew that before you told me'.

examples.text: *A:* I found that lecture really boring. *B:* **So I gather**. I saw you sleeping.
*A:* Maria's not very well. *B:* **So I understand**. / **So she tells me**.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Will you be able to come over this weekend? *B:* I hope ___.
exercises.explanation: Hope is one of the thinking verbs that take so instead of a whole clause.

exercises.prompt: *A:* The weather's awful, so we'll need to take a taxi. *B:* I guess ___.
exercises.explanation: Positive replies with guess take so; in the negative only 'I guess not' is possible.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Will we need to pay to get in? *B:* ___
exercises.explanation: Doubt is never followed by so - use I doubt it or I doubt (that) we will.

exercises.prompt: *A:* You will remember to pick me up at one, won't you? *B:* I promise ___.
exercises.explanation: Promise is not used with so, so we spell the clause out: I promise (that) I will.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I hope I'll be able to get a ticket. *B:* I'm sure ___.
exercises.explanation: Be sure does not take so, so the clause is spelt out: I'm sure (that) you will.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Did I leave my handbag in your car yesterday? *B:* ___
exercises.explanation: With think we prefer not ... so. 'I think not' is possible but rather formal.

exercises.statement: *A:* Didn't Alice hear you? *B:* It doesn't appear.
exercises.explanation: It doesn't appear so. / It appears not. With appear we need either not ... so or not on its own.

exercises.prompt: *A:* What did you think of Sadia's work? *B:* Well, I thought it was pretty awful, although I ___.
exercises.explanation: 'I didn't say so' = I didn't tell them my opinion; 'said not' would mean the opposite of what B thinks.

exercises.prompt: *A:* The children from next door are taking the apples from our trees. *B:* ___ I said they could come round and get them.
exercises.explanation: B knew about it before being told, so a 'So ...' answer is not possible here.

exercises.prompt: *A:* The DVD player's gone again. *B:* So ___ . Dr Adams has probably borrowed it.
exercises.explanation: So + pronoun + the auxiliary from A's sentence (has): B can see it is true now.

exercises.prompt: Say that the workers were right to feel as they did, without repeating the adjective.
exercises.answer: The workers were angry and they had every right to be so.
exercises.explanation: So stands for the adjective angry.

exercises.prompt: Match each reply with what it tells us.

pairs.left: *A:* Lisa and Sara are here. *B:* So they are.
pairs.right: I can see that is true now you have told me.

pairs.left: *A:* Your bike's been moved. *B:* Yes, it has. Philip borrowed it this morning.
pairs.right: I knew about it before you told me.

pairs.left: *A:* I found that lecture really boring. *B:* So I gather.
pairs.right: I already knew - I saw you sleeping.

pairs.left: *A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher said not.
pairs.right: The teacher said we didn't have to.

pairs.left: *A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher said not to.
*A:* Do we have to do all ten questions? *B:* The teacher didn't say so.
pairs.right: The teacher didn't tell us to - but perhaps we should.
